dataset.what_one_row_represents: A single officiating decision (correct call, correct non-call, incorrect call, or incorrect non-call) reviewed by the NBA in the last two minutes of a close game
dataset.cleaning_note: 1,765 rows dropped because review_decision contained stray player names rather than the four valid codes CC/CNC/IC/INC

ana_01.label: Overall CC / CNC / IC / INC split
ana_01.content: Of 25,057 NBA-reviewed late-game decisions from March 2015 through June 2018, the league classified 29.58% as Correct Calls (CC, 7,412 plays), 61.65% as Correct Non-Calls (CNC, 15,448 plays), 0.96% as Incorrect Calls (IC, 240 plays), and 7.81% as Incorrect Non-Calls (INC, 1,957 plays). Overall correctness is 91.23%. Missed whistles (INC) outnumber wrongful whistles (IC) by 8.2 to 1 — the league's late-game errors are overwhelmingly errors of omission.

data_table.description: The four review-decision categories and their shares of all 25,057 reviewed plays.

ana_02.label: Errors per game distribution
ana_02.content: Across 1,473 L2M-reviewed games, the mean number of referee errors (IC+INC combined) per game is 1.49 and the median is 1. Only 28.9% of games (426) had zero errors; 3.6% (53 games) had five or more errors. The worst game had 14 errors. A typical close NBA game ends with one or two decisions the league will later admit were wrong.

ana_03.label: Error rate by call type
ana_03.content: Error rates vary wildly by call type. Defensive 3-second violations are missed 63.6% of the time (140 INC of 220 total), and traveling violations are missed 43.9% of the time (237 INC of 539 total). At the other extreme, shooting fouls and personal fouls — the bread-and-butter calls — are officiated correctly 93-95% of the time. The obscure, process-heavy violations are where the crew gets sloppy; the high-consequence contact calls get attention.

ana_04.label: Call type volume in crunch time
ana_04.content: Personal fouls (7,522) and shooting fouls (6,962) are by far the most common reviewed calls in the final two minutes — together they account for 57.7% of all L2M plays. Offensive fouls and loose-ball fouls round out the top four. Traveling, defensive 3-second, and turnover violations combined make up less than 5% of reviewed plays despite their outsized error rates.

ana_05.label: Most-worked referees and their error rates
ana_05.content: Scott Foster — the referee voted worst in the league by anonymous player surveys — leads all officials with 94 L2M-reviewed games and 1,599 plays judged. His error rate of 9.82% is noticeably above the league median of 8.83% for refs with 40+ games. Among the top 15 most-worked refs, Tom Washington (10.36%), Leroy Richardson (10.18%), and Josh Tiven (10.28%) have higher error rates than Foster; Bill Kennedy (6.85%) and Tony Brothers (8.30%) have notably lower rates. The spread among the league's most-used referees is narrow but real.

ana_07.label: Scott Foster's specific numbers
ana_07.content: Scott Foster — the ref Chris Paul publicly feuds with and who players vote the worst in the league — worked 94 L2M games (the league high) and had 1,599 reviewed plays. His breakdown: 515 correct calls, 927 correct non-calls, 17 incorrect calls, and 140 incorrect non-calls. His 9.82% error rate ranks 49th out of 59 eligible referees (1st = cleanest). He is worse than league median but not an outlier — ten referees are measurably worse. The reputation far exceeds what the data alone can justify.

ana_08.label: Home vs away team error split (no meaningful bias)
ana_08.content: Across 2,165 errors where the hurt team is identifiable, the home team was disadvantaged 1,080 times (49.88%) and the away team 1,085 times (50.12%). A five-call difference across the entire four-season dataset. On incorrect calls (wrongful whistles, n=225) there is a faint lean toward hurting the home team (52.89% home vs 47.11% away — 13 extra calls); on incorrect non-calls (missed whistles, n=1,940) away teams are hurt slightly more (50.46% vs 49.54%). Neither lean is statistically meaningful. The folklore that L2M data proves home-court bias is not supported in this time window.

ana_10.label: Players most disadvantaged by referee errors
ana_10.content: Andrew Wiggins has the most negative net in the league: 22 times disadvantaged by errors, 7 times the beneficiary — a net of -15 calls over his 335 L2M appearances. Damian Lillard (-14), Isaiah Thomas (-13), Kemba Walker (-12), and Gordon Hayward (-11) round out the top five. LeBron James also tilts negative (25 disadvantaged, 20 committing — net -5) across 477 appearances. These are guards and wings — the kind of players whose close-game drives are most likely to draw hard-to-officiate contact. Superstar treatment, if it exists, is not landing here.

ana_11.label: Players most advantaged (big men commit more than they suffer)

ana_12.label: Error rate by seconds-left (the buzzer effect reversed)
ana_12.content: Intuition says mistakes get worse under pressure as the clock winds down. The data says the opposite: error rate drops to 6.62% in the last 10 seconds (27 IC, 236 INC out of 3,972 decisions), compared with 8-10% everywhere else in the two-minute window. The 40-49 second bucket has the single highest error rate at 10.07%. One plausible reading: referees call fewer speculative whistles — more ball stays inbounds, more timeouts are used, more action is dead — as the buzzer approaches, so the decisions that survive are easier ones.

data_table.description: Error rate by 10-second bucket of time remaining in Q4/OT.

ana_13.label: Volume spike in the final 30 seconds
ana_13.content: The final 30 seconds of a close game accounts for 9,363 reviewed decisions — about 37% of the entire dataset despite being only 25% of the two-minute window. Reviewed decisions in the 0-9s bucket (3,972) are more than double those in any 10-second bucket before 30s. More calls, more pressure, more scrutiny — the density of reviewed events explodes as the ball finds its way to the last scoring possession.

data_table.description: Number of reviewed decisions in each 10-second bucket of the final two minutes.

ana_14.label: Error rate cut in half over four seasons
ana_14.content: The league has measurably gotten better. Error rate fell from 13.03% in the partial 2014-15 season to 11.52% in 2015-16, 8.62% in 2016-17, and 6.15% in 2017-18 — less than half the inaugural rate. Errors per game dropped from 1.84 to 1.27 on the same trajectory. Either the league's expansion of reviewed eligibility in 2017-18 is catching easier decisions (diluting the error rate), the crew is actually improving under scrutiny, or both. Absolute IC and INC counts also fell even as total reviewed plays rose from 6,830 to 9,698.

data_table.description: Error rate and errors-per-game by NBA season.

ana_15.label: Worst-officiated games in L2M history
ana_15.content: The single worst-refereed close game in the dataset is Wolves at Wizards on March 25, 2016 — 14 referee errors called out by the league, with Mike Callahan, Josh Tiven, and Justin Van Duyne working the crew. Second-worst is Knicks at Hawks on January 29, 2017, with 11 errors and a crew that included Scott Foster. Third is Nuggets at Pelicans on March 15, 2015, with 10 errors — also a Scott Foster game. Foster appears on two of the three worst-officiated games in the dataset, more than any other referee.

ana_17.label: The missed-whistle-vs-wrong-whistle asymmetry
ana_17.content: Of the 1,957 incorrect non-calls, 382 (19.5%) were missed shooting fouls, 349 were missed offensive fouls, 339 were missed personal fouls, and 237 were missed traveling violations. Of the 240 incorrect calls, 103 (42.9%) were wrongful shooting-foul whistles and 69 were wrongful personal fouls. Shooting fouls dominate both error columns — unsurprising given contact near the basket is both frequent and ambiguous.

caveats.content: The L2M scope expanded in the 2017-18 season to include any game in which the lead was 3 or fewer at ANY point in the final two minutes. Earlier seasons only qualified when the lead was 3 or fewer at the 2:00 mark. Year-over-year totals are therefore not fully comparable — per-game normalization is safer than raw counts.

1,765 raw rows (6.6%) were dropped because the review_decision field contained a player name instead of one of the valid CC/CNC/IC/INC codes — a data-quality artifact of the PDF-to-CSV pipeline. This is unlikely to bias aggregate percentages but means absolute totals differ slightly from the README summary.

The NBA only publishes L2Ms for games within 3 points. Blowouts are not sampled. The error rate observed here — 8.77% — is specific to the final two minutes of close games, not typical of the whole game or the full season.

CNC (Correct Non-Call) counts only include non-calls the league flagged as worth reviewing. Many legitimate non-calls are never reviewed. The true denominator of 'correct decisions' is larger than what the L2M records, which the league has repeatedly pointed out when defending referee performance.
